name: Raw milk for height
lead: Raw milk for height is the practice of drinking unpasteurised milk in the hope of growing taller or filling out one's frame. It appears in height-focused and looksmaxxing circles alongside slogans such as "Raw Milk + Healthy = Holy Height", and is often grouped with primal and carnivore-style diets. The appearance goal is straightforward: milk supplies protein, calcium and fat-soluble vitamins, and adherents treat it as a growth-supporting food for people who are still growing.[3][4]

Dairy and height are linked at the population level. Wikipedia's article on human height reports that nations eating more protein from meat, dairy, eggs and fish tend to be taller than those relying on cereal protein, and that historically cattle-rich, high-dairy populations were taller.[2] That association concerns dairy generally, not raw milk specifically. Twin studies put the heritability of height at roughly 60 to 80 percent, and growth typically ends in the late teens.[2]

Raw milk itself is milk that has not been heat-treated. Proponents say it tastes better, is more nutritious and supports immunity.[1] A 2011 systematic review and meta-analysis of 40 studies on vitamins found that pasteurisation lowered some vitamins (B1, B2, C, folate) while the overall effect on nutritive value was reported as minimal, and it did not find support for several advocacy claims.[5] The CDC and FDA advise against drinking raw milk because it can carry pathogens, and legal access varies by country and US state.[1] No published study has measured height outcomes in people drinking raw versus pasteurised milk.

angle.text: Adherents drink raw milk as a nutrient-dense food they associate with growth, hoping to maximise height while growth plates are still open. Dairy-rich diets are linked with taller populations in general, though that research does not distinguish raw from pasteurised milk.

paras: Raw milk is milk sold or consumed without pasteurisation. Wikipedia reports that proponents credit it with better flavour, more nutrition, immune support and protection against allergies.[1] In looksmaxxing forums the milk is usually discussed together with raw meat, liver and eggs as part of a primal-diet approach, and sometimes as a way to improve skin, hormones or bone structure.[7][8]

Wikipedia's article on human height notes that average national height correlates with protein quality, and that populations with many cattle and high dairy intake were historically taller, citing the early nineteenth-century US, Argentina, New Zealand and Australia.[2] It also states that malnutrition is linked to stunted growth.[2]

Height is highly heritable (about 60 to 80 percent in twin studies), and growth in males typically finishes around 18 to 19.[2] Forum users who discuss the topic frequently point to growth plate fusion as the point after which diet is not expected to change height.[7]

The 2011 meta-analysis in the Journal of Food Protection found that pasteurisation decreased vitamins B1, B2, C and folate, that B12 and E fell and vitamin A rose qualitatively, and concluded that the effect on milk's nutritive value was minimal.[5] Wikipedia reports a 2012 Belgian review reaching a similar conclusion and notes that the FDA says pasteurisation does not destroy nutritional value.[1]
Forum posters on looksmax.org argue the opposite: one thread claims raw milk keeps vitamins, enzymes and whey protein intact and may support hormones and, in the young, height.[6]

A review of raw milk's microbiota lists Listeria, Salmonella, E. coli and Campylobacter among the organisms that can occur in it.[9] Wikipedia lists additional hazards including Brucella and tuberculosis, with children under five, people over 65, pregnant women and the immunocompromised at highest risk, and notes possible complications such as haemolytic-uremic syndrome and Guillain-Barre syndrome.[1]

Reviews have also described raw-milk transmission of tick-borne encephalitis virus and brucellosis.[10][11] The CDC and FDA strongly advise against drinking raw milk.[1] A Hacker News thread discussed reports of cats developing H5N1 infections after drinking raw milk, and Wikipedia notes H5N1 has been detected in US milk supplies.[1][12]

Wikipedia reports that about 43 US states permit some form of raw milk sale, often via farm sales or herdshares; direct sale is federally prohibited in Canada; in the UK about 150 producers sell "green top" milk directly; and it is illegal for drinking in Australia, where it is sometimes sold as bath milk.[1]

Looksmax.org threads show both enthusiasm and scepticism. Some members promote raw milk as a looksmax in its own right, others ask whether it is worthwhile, and others discuss where to obtain it.[6][13] Sceptical posters argue that bone structure is set once growth plates fuse and that raw milk and raw-food diets will not reshape the face; they recommend eating a normal healthy diet instead.[7]

No studies found on raw milk and height. Related research includes the 2011 meta-analysis of pasteurisation and vitamin levels, which also assessed advocacy claims about allergy and other outcomes.[5] A randomised trial letter examined yoghurt as an alternative to raw milk for infant eczema and allergy, which concerns allergy rather than growth.[14]

lore.intro: On looksmax.org, raw milk is debated as a height and bone-structure aid, usually within broader raw-food and carnivore diet discussion.[6][7]

claims.claim: Raw milk is more nutritious than pasteurised milk
claims.believers: A poster argues pasteurisation destroys enzymes and reduces vitamins and whey protein, so raw milk supports skin, hormones and height in the young.[6]
claims.experts: A 2011 meta-analysis found some vitamins fall with pasteurisation but nutritive value is minimally affected.[5]

claims.claim: Raw milk helps people grow taller
claims.believers: Members suggest dairy's protein and nutrients, and possibly growth-hormone effects, help growth in the young.[6]
claims.experts: Population studies link dairy-rich diets with taller populations, but no study has compared raw and pasteurised milk and height.[2]

claims.claim: Raw milk and primal diets can reshape facial bones
claims.believers: Some posters say raw milk, raw meat and liver can improve recessed midface features.[7]
claims.experts: Other forum members counter that growth plates fuse in the late teens and diet will not change a finished skeleton; no studies have tested the claim.[7]

claims.believers: Raw-milk supporters in the thread acknowledge bacterial risk from poor sources.[6]
claims.experts: The CDC and FDA advise against raw milk because of pathogens such as Listeria, Salmonella and E. coli.[1][9]

card.summary: Drinking unpasteurised milk to grow taller; no height studies exist and the CDC and FDA advise against it.
card.note: CDC and FDA strongly recommend against raw milk; documented outbreaks.

quick.overview:
Raw milk for height is the belief that unpasteurised milk helps people grow taller. Reference sources show dairy-rich diets track with taller populations but do not single out raw milk.

No study of raw milk and height was found.
quick.mechanism: Believers point to the protein and nutrients in milk. Sources report heating does not substantially change nutritional value.
quick.risks: The CDC and FDA recommend against raw milk because it can carry pathogens such as Listeria, Salmonella and E. coli, with highest risk in young children, older adults, pregnancy and weakened immunity. Legal status varies by country and US state.
